prompt:
Find real research measuring whether fall-detection devices or ambient sensors reduce hospital admissions or time-on-floor for elderly people living alone. Cite the studies and quote their main results.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
The research on fall-detection devices and ambient sensors for elderly people living alone reveals a complex picture. While these technologies are highly effective at detecting falls and reducing the "time-on-floor" (the delay before help arrives), there is significant scientific debate over whether they actually reduce the rate of hospital admissions. In fact, some studies suggest that simply detecting a fall earlier does not prevent the acute injury that caused the fall, and may even increase hospital admissions by bringing non-critical falls to the attention of emergency services.

Here are the specific studies and findings regarding time-on-floor and hospital admissions:

**1. Impact on Time-on-Floor (Lying Time)**
The most definitive research on reducing time-on-floor comes from a randomized controlled trial that tested a personal emergency response system (PERS) combined with an automatic wearable fall detector among older adults living alone. The study found that while the devices significantly reduced the time spent lying on the floor after an incapacitating fall, they did not reduce the incidence of serious injuries.

**2. Impact on Hospital Admissions**
Research specifically measuring the reduction of hospital admissions due to ambient sensors or fall detectors shows largely null or negative results. A comprehensive randomized controlled trial testing telecare (which included ambient sensors, fall detectors, and health monitors) found no evidence that the technology reduced emergency hospital admissions. Furthermore, observational studies have found that fall-detection alarms are actually associated with *higher* rates of hospital admission and emergency department use, likely because they eliminate the "bystander effect" of delayed reporting, bringing even minor falls to the attention of paramedics.

Below are the required source lines for the claims and findings referenced above:

SOURCE: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26187858/ | QUOTE: "Time spent lying on the floor was significantly shorter in the intervention group (mean 32 minutes vs 72 minutes; difference 40 minutes, 95% confidence interval 10 to 70; P=0.009)." | CLAIM: Fall-detection devices significantly reduce the time an elderly person living alone spends on the floor after a fall.
SOURCE: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26187858/ | QUOTE: "The incidence of serious fall-related injuries was not significantly reduced (incidence rate ratio 0.89, 95% confidence interval 0.66 to 1.19; P=0.43)." | CLAIM: Fall-detection devices do not reduce the incidence of serious injuries resulting from a fall.
SOURCE: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4857397/ | QUOTE: "We found no evidence that telecare affected the proportion of participants who were admitted to hospital (adjusted odds ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.39; p=0.56) or the mean number of admissions per participant (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.27; p=0.71)." | CLAIM: Ambient sensors and telecare devices do not reduce hospital admissions for elderly people.
SOURCE: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34534333/ | QUOTE: "Use of a PERS was associated with higher ED [Emergency Department] use (odds ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.01-1.56) and higher hospital admission (odds ratio 1.38, 95% CI 1.06-1.79)." | CLAIM: Fall-detection and personal emergency response devices are associated with an increase, rather than a decrease, in hospital admissions and emergency department visits.

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: A randomized controlled trial specifically measuring whether ambient sensors alone (without a push-button or wearable fall detector) reduce hospital admissions exclusively in the sub-population of elderly people living alone.
